note:
v1, THE SKELETON of "False Summit" (track 5; your words: "true djent ... audio illusions throughout mainly risers/shpehers ... a clear illlusory song, all about the illusions"). 4:24, 100 bpm, in F. The title is mine: a false summit is the top you can see from below that is not the top.
THE IDEA: the illusions are played BY THE BAND, not by a pad behind it.
- THE STAIR (0:19): a line over the low chug climbs the scale an octave every bar and never gets higher. Four guitars a side play it an octave apart, each fading in at the bottom and out at the top. Every bar is the same bar; every bar starts higher than the last.
- THE TURN (1:17): the low chug at three speeds at once, all speeding up; the fastest fades out as a slower one fades in. Faster and faster, never faster. The kit holds the bar, and every fourth bar line they are together again.
- THE DESCENT (1:55): the stair downwards and all of it: the whole riff a step lower every bar. A tuning that keeps dropping.
- THE POLE (2:53): a breath. One chord through a filter that climbs for ever, and a bass that is only its overtones.
- BOTH (3:22): pitch and speed rise together, like a tape speeding up, under a riser that never arrives. It stops dead.
- THE SUMMIT (4:02): a bar of nothing, then the first bars again, exactly. After all that climbing the band is where it started.

TWO QUESTIONS ON THE PAGE, because I cannot hear whether an illusion works: does the riff keep climbing or do you hear it drop back; does the chug keep getting faster.
WHAT I MEASURED (I did not listen): compscore 98.36 / 99.10 (seeds 0 and 11). File -10.0 LUFS.
- Each guitar's fader follows its bell note by note, after the amp. The eight together hold the same level and tone from bar to bar (within 1 dB), which is what makes a bar that climbs an octave the same bar.
- In the turn the same notes fall at the same times in every four-bar cycle, whichever guitar plays them.
- The parts that carry an illusion are 1.8 LU under the whole mix and near the front for the whole song (the guitars alone: 84% of it).
- Full sections are -16.0 to -17.3 on the groove; the pole is 3 dB under them.
BARE, AS A SKELETON IS: one riff in the stair for 24 bars; the kit only keeps time; no tune yet beyond the line; not yet read against the records.
NOT HEARD BY ANYONE. Whether any of it sounds endless is the whole question.

note:
v2, THE ILLUSIONS HOLD, AND THE JOINS ARE RISERS (whole song, as drawn). No answers yet on the two cards, so nothing here changes what they ask.
1. THE JOINS ARE RISERS, ON THE GUITARS (you asked for "mainly risers/shpehers but in djent style"). Three sections now hand over on a run: the eight guitars pick a semitone to the sixteenth, climbing and never higher. Into the turn (1:12), out of the pole into both (3:17, under the riser), and falling out of the descent (2:48). Under the rising ones the snare doubles its speed.
2. EVERY BAR IS NOW THE SAME BAR. chirp-eco built a tool that measures whether an illusion holds. It found the stair repeated every FOUR bars, not every bar: each of the eight guitars had its own speaker and its own place in the stereo, so which speaker held which octave came round. And the turn's last two cycles were 2 dB louder than its first two. The four guitars a side now share one speaker and one place.
3. A TICK THAT SPEEDS UP FOR EVER, in the pole (2:53): the hat, on the engine's own endless rhythm. The plain form of the turn, heard alone.
4. THE FIRST READ AGAINST THE RECORDS, by part. The stair was 3.7 dB over them at 250-500 Hz and the plain tone held most of it: it is 2.5 dB down under the band. Under the turn the bass held one long note a bar, which is all low-mid and no weight: it now strikes every beat, with the kit.

note:
v3, THE STAIR HAS A TUNE (whole song, as drawn). No answers yet on the three cards; the passages they ask about keep their notes.
1. A TUNE. The line the guitars climb was the scale, straight up: the plain form of the illusion, and not a tune. It still is for the first eight bars with the band. Then, at 0:38, it becomes a figure: up two notes of the scale, back one, up two, back one, each bar starting higher than the last. It is two bars long, ends an octave above where it began, and begins again there: so it climbs an octave every two bars and is never higher. The kit takes the backbeat where it comes in.
2. THE EIGHT GUITARS' HONK. Read against the eleven records, the stair was 3.7 dB over them at 500 Hz-1 kHz, and it was the eight guitars. One tone control on each takes 2.5 dB off there.

note:
v4, THE LEAD COMES DOWN (section round, 0:57-1:12, as drawn: the stair's last six bars before the run; the map called the stretch static, and from the band's entry at 0:19 to the turn at 1:16 nothing new came in).
A lead guitar now comes in over the tune and does the one thing nothing else in this song does: it really moves. It comes DOWN the scale, a note to the half bar, two octaves in six bars, and lands on the low F exactly where the guitars' run begins. In those six bars the tune under it climbs three octaves and is no higher; the lead falls two and is two octaves lower. So the one honest line in the song shows the stair up for what it is.
